lead: Concrete is strong in compression and weak in tension; steel is strong in tension and ductile, so steel bars are placed where concrete would crack. Every design method starts from how each material behaves when squeezed or stretched: its strength, its stiffness and the strain at which it gives up. This chapter reads the stress–strain curves of concrete and reinforcing steel as IS 456:2000 idealises them, defines f<sub>ck</sub> and f<sub>y</sub>, and adds the slow effects, creep and shrinkage, that change a member over its life.
prereq: You need: stress, strain, Hooke's law and the second moment of area from engineering mechanics.

blocks.text: Concrete is cement, sand, coarse aggregate and water hardened into a stony mass. Its tensile strength is only about a tenth of its compressive strength, so steel is placed wherever tension occurs.

Strength is measured by crushing 150 mm cubes after 28 days of curing. The grade M20, M25, M30 names the characteristic cube strength fck in N/mm²: M25 means fck = 25 N/mm². "Characteristic" means that not more than 5 % of the test results are expected to fall below this value (see characteristic strength and loads). A cylinder 150 mm across and 300 mm tall breaks at about 0.8 times the cube strength, because the steel platens of the machine hold the short cube and make it look stronger.
IS 456 sets a minimum grade for reinforced concrete by exposure: M20 for mild exposure, M25 for moderate, M30 for severe, M35 for very severe and M40 for extreme.

Two more properties come from f<sub>ck</sub>. The short-term modulus of elasticity is E<sub>c</sub> = 5000 √f<sub>ck</sub>, and the flexural tensile strength (modulus of rupture) is f<sub>cr</sub> = 0.7 √f<sub>ck</sub>, both in N/mm².

The real compressive curve climbs, bends over, peaks near a strain of 0.002 and then falls as the concrete crushes. For design IS 456 replaces it with an idealised curve: a parabola from zero to a strain of 0.002, then a flat line up to the ultimate strain 0.0035. In the member the flat part is at 0.67fck; with the material factor 1.5 it becomes 0.67fck/1.5 = 0.446fck, the design curve used at collapse (see stress block parameters).

sections.h3: Reinforcing steel: grades and design curves

blocks.text: Bars are graded by their characteristic yield strength f<sub>y</sub> in N/mm². Mild steel Fe250 is a plain bar with a sharp yield point; high yield strength deformed (HYSD) bars, Fe415, Fe500 and Fe550, carry ribs that grip the concrete. "Fe" is the chemical symbol for iron (Latin ferrum); Fe415 means f<sub>y</sub> = 415 N/mm², not a design stress of 415 N/mm². For bars with no sharp yield point, f<sub>y</sub> is the 0.2 % proof stress: the stress that leaves a permanent strain of 0.002 when the load is removed.

All grades have the same modulus, E<sub>s</sub> = 2 × 10⁵ N/mm², about eight times the modulus of M25 concrete. Higher grades need less bar area but are less ductile: the minimum elongation at fracture is 14.5 % for Fe415 and 12 % for Fe500.
IS 456 gives two design curves, both with a design yield stress f<sub>yd</sub> = f<sub>y</sub>/1.15 = 0.87f<sub>y</sub>.

items: Mild steel (Fe250): a straight line up to 0.87fy = 217.5 N/mm² at a strain of 217.5 / 200,000 = 0.00109, then flat.
HYSD bars (Fe415, Fe500): straight only up to 0.8 × 0.87fy. Beyond it the curve bends, and 0.87fy is reached at an extra inelastic strain of 0.002, that is at a total strain of 0.87fy/Es + 0.002.

blocks.text: SP 16, the design aid to IS 456, tabulates this curve: for Fe415 it runs from 288.7 N/mm² at a strain of 0.00144 to 360.9 N/mm² at 0.00380. So Fe415 reaches its full design stress only at a strain of 0.0038. Fe500 reaches it at 0.87 × 500 / 200,000 + 0.002 = 0.00418.

Creep is the slow growth of strain under a load that stays on. The creep coefficient θ is the final creep strain divided by the elastic strain. IS 456 gives θ = 2.2 when the load is first applied at 7 days, 1.6 at 28 days and 1.1 at one year: the older the concrete when loaded, the less it creeps. Creep is handled through an effective modulus Ece = Ec/(1 + θ).

Shrinkage is the drying contraction of concrete with no load on it; IS 456 suggests a total shrinkage strain of 0.0003 in the absence of test data. Both add to the deflection of a slab over the years.

Durability is the ability of concrete to protect its steel from water and chlorides, which make bars rust, swell and split the cover. IS 456 fixes the nominal cover by exposure: 20 mm for mild, 30 mm for moderate, 45 mm for severe, 50 mm for very severe and 75 mm for extreme exposure, along with a maximum water–cement ratio and a minimum cement content.
The strains 0.002 and 0.0035 build the stress block, and Ec, θ and the shrinkage strain give the deflections checked at the limit state of serviceability.

examples.question: A beam 230 mm wide and 450 mm deep overall is made of M25 concrete and reinforced with Fe415 bars. (a) Find the short-term modulus E<sub>c</sub> and the flexural tensile strength f<sub>cr</sub>. (b) Find the bending moment at which the uncracked beam first cracks; ignore the steel. (c) Find the strain at which the bars reach their design stress 0.87f<sub>y</sub>, and compare it with the strain of Fe250.
steps: Grade M25 gives f<sub>ck</sub> = 25 N/mm², so √f<sub>ck</sub> = 5.
Section modulus of the gross section: Z = b D²/6 = 230 × 450² / 6 = 7.7625 × 10⁶ mm³ (I = 1.7466 × 10⁹ mm⁴ divided by 225 mm).
Cracking moment M<sub>cr</sub> = f<sub>cr</sub> × Z = 3.5 × 7.7625 × 10⁶ = 27.17 × 10⁶ Nmm = 27.2 kNm.
Fe415 design stress 0.87 × 415 = 361.05 N/mm². Elastic part of the strain = 361.05 / 200,000 = 0.0018; add the inelastic 0.002: total 0.0038.
examples.answer: E<sub>c</sub> = 25,000 N/mm², f<sub>cr</sub> = 3.5 N/mm²; the beam cracks at about 27.2 kNm; Fe415 reaches 0.87f<sub>y</sub> at a strain of 0.0038, against 0.00109 for Fe250.

examples.question: M25 concrete in a column, loaded at 28 days, carries a sustained stress of 6 N/mm². Find the elastic, creep and total long-term strains (with shrinkage) and the effective modulus. How does the creep change if the load comes on at 7 days?
steps: E<sub>c</sub> = 25,000 N/mm² (first worked example). Elastic strain = 6 / 25,000 = 0.00024.
Loading at 28 days: θ = 1.6. Creep strain = 1.6 × 0.00024 = 0.000384.
With shrinkage 0.0003: total = 0.00024 + 0.000384 + 0.0003 = 0.000924, almost four times the elastic strain.
Effective modulus E<sub>ce</sub> = E<sub>c</sub>/(1 + θ) = 25,000 / 2.6 = 9615 N/mm².
At 7 days θ = 2.2: creep strain 2.2 × 0.00024 = 0.000528, 37.5 % more; older concrete creeps less.
examples.answer: Elastic 0.00024, creep 0.000384, total 0.000924; E<sub>ce</sub> = 9615 N/mm²; 0.000528 creep if loaded at 7 days.

traps: E<sub>c</sub> is not f<sub>ck</sub>. For M25, f<sub>ck</sub> = 25 N/mm² while E<sub>c</sub> = 25,000 N/mm², a thousand times larger; both are in N/mm², which hides the slip.
The design stress of Fe415 is 0.87 × 415 = 361 N/mm², not 415 N/mm²; see partial safety factors.

For HYSD bars the design stress is reached at a strain of 0.87f<sub>y</sub>/Es + 0.002 (0.0038 for Fe415), not at 0.87f<sub>y</sub>/Es (0.0018). Using 0.0018 gives a wrong limiting depth of neutral axis.
Creep coefficients are 2.2, 1.6 and 1.1 for loading at 7 days, 28 days and one year; using 2.2 at 28 days overstates long-term deflection by 3.2/2.6 = 1.23 times.

quiz.q: Define the characteristic compressive strength f<sub>ck</sub> of concrete.
quiz.a: The compressive strength of 150 mm cubes at 28 days below which not more than 5 % of the test results are expected to fall, in N/mm².

quiz.q: State the IS 456 expressions for E<sub>c</sub> and f<sub>cr</sub> in terms of f<sub>ck</sub>.
quiz.a: E<sub>c</sub> = 5000 √f<sub>ck</sub> and f<sub>cr</sub> = 0.7 √f<sub>ck</sub>, both in N/mm².

quiz.q: Why does IS 456 use the 0.2 % proof stress as f<sub>y</sub> for Fe415 bars?
quiz.a: HYSD bars have no sharp yield point; the curve bends gradually. The 0.2 % proof stress, the stress that leaves a permanent strain of 0.002, gives a repeatable value to call the yield strength.

quiz.q: Find the strain at which Fe500 bars reach their design stress.
An M20 beam 300 mm wide and 600 mm deep: find its cracking moment.
A slab is redesigned from Fe415 to Fe500 bars for the same ultimate moment. What changes, and what must be watched?
quiz.a: The bar area falls to about 415/500 = 0.83 times. But Fe500 needs a larger strain (0.00418 against 0.0038) to reach its design stress and is less ductile (12 % elongation against 14.5 %), so the limiting neutral axis depth is smaller. Check crack width, deflection and bond length, since the service steel stress is higher.

beyond: High-strength concretes above M60 have a more brittle curve than the IS 456 parabola, and newer codes treat them separately. Thermo-mechanically treated (TMT) bars are now the usual Fe500 bar on Indian sites, and the Fe500D and Fe550D grades add ductility rules for earthquake zones. Search next for "TMT bar IS 1786" and "creep prediction model".

figure.caption: The design curves of the worked example. Left: M25 concrete rises as a parabola to a strain of 0.002 and stays flat to 0.0035; the dashed curve is 0.67f<sub>ck</sub> before the material factor. Right: Fe415 leaves the straight line at 0.8 × 0.87f<sub>y</sub> and reaches 361 N/mm² only at a strain of 0.0038, while Fe250 has a sharp corner at 217.5 N/mm².
